idiom_name: ASP.NET Core policies (requirements + handlers) over ClaimsPrincipal, with object-level IAuthorizationService checks
implementation_notes: The framework ships the decision and the grant model: an endpoint declares the authority it requires (RequireAuthorization with a policy name, or the Authorize attribute with Policy = ...), a policy is a named set of requirements that must all pass, and a handler resolves each requirement against the ClaimsPrincipal. What replaces a hand-written rights table is that pairing - the requirement type is the grant, the handler is the check - while the host identity (application pool account, service account, container user, workload identity) carries the operating-system grant set. The framework-era sandbox is not part of modern .NET (Code Access Security was not carried forward), so the process identity and the platform are the enforcement boundary, and the policy layer decides requests above it. The classic form is still justified for rules that depend on the resource rather than the caller: use IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(user, resource, policy) at the point of access, because an attribute on the action only authorizes the request, not the row it loads.
pitfalls: An attribute on the action authorizes the request, not the object: object-level rules need AuthorizeAsync with the resource, otherwise a caller who holds the scope reaches any id it can guess.

Requirements inside one policy are ANDed, which fails safe in the tightening direction but silently locks legitimate callers out when a requirement lands on the wrong policy; test the policy set, not just the handler.

The host identity is the other half of the grant: a correctly authorized application that runs as db_owner or as a local administrator still has the deployment's authority, because the policy layer decides the request while the identity decides the blast radius.
